N1.text: April 1973. The first picture on a Xerox Alto: Cookie Monster. Every pixel, fed to the screen by its one and only processor.

check.transcript: April 1973. The first picture on a Xerox Alto: Cookie Monster. Every pixel, fed to the screen by its one and only processor.

N2.text: The Alto's device boards are mostly buffers and shift registers. The rest — every disk word, every packet, every scanline — is microcode.

check.transcript: The Alto's device boards are mostly buffers and shift registers. The rest, every disk word, every packet, every scanline, is microcode.

N3.text: Every 170 nanoseconds, it runs one 32-bit microinstruction: register, ALU op, bus source, two functions… and the address of the next one.

check.transcript: Every 170 nanoseconds, it runs one 32-bit microinstruction: register, ALU op, bus source, two functions, and the address of the next one.

N4.text: There's no program counter to increment. Every instruction names its successor, and a branch just ORs a bit into that address.

check.transcript: There's no program counter to increment. Every instruction names its successor, and a branch just ORs a bit into that address.

N5.text: Even the instruction set programmers saw — a Data General Nova lookalike — is just a microcode program. An ADD is eight microinstructions: 1.36 microseconds. A real Nova 1200 took 1.35.

check.transcript: Even the instruction set programmers saw, a Data General Nova lookalike, is just a microcode program. An ADD is eight microinstructions: 1.36 microseconds. A real Nova 1200 took 1.35.

N6.text: That emulator is task zero: the lowest of sixteen priorities.

check.transcript: That emulator is task zero, the lowest of sixteen priorities.

N7.text: Each task has its own micro-PC. Devices raise wakeup lines, a priority encoder picks the winner, and the running task yields whenever it says TASK. Nothing is saved, so switching is free.

check.transcript: Each task has its own micro-PC. Devices raise wakeup lines, a priority encoder picks the winner, and the running task yields whenever it says TASK. Nothing is saved, so switching is free.

N8.text: Priority follows buffering: the disk holds one word, so it outranks everything. The Ethernet holds sixteen, so it can wait.

check.transcript: Priority follows buffering. The disk holds one word, so it outranks everything. The Ethernet holds sixteen, so it can wait.

N9.text: The screen is a 606 by 808 bitmap — nearly half of main memory.

check.transcript: The screen is a 606 by 808 bitmap, nearly half of main memory.

N10.text: The clock was picked so a scanline is exactly 224 cycles. And memory's too slow for single words, so the display reads two at a time: thirty-two pixels every six microinstructions.

check.transcript: The clock was picked so a scanline is exactly 224 cycles. And memory's too slow for single words, so the display reads two at a time: 32 pixels every six microinstructions.

N11.text: On each visible line, the display takes sixty percent of the cycles, memory refresh about a tenth — and your program gets the rest: about a third.

check.transcript: On each visible line, the display takes 60% of the cycles, memory refresh about a tenth, and your program gets the rest: about a third.

N12.text: Even DRAM refresh is microcode — and on its way through, that task counts the mouse.

check.transcript: Even DRAM refresh is microcode, and on its way through, that task counts the mouse.

N13.text: The disk task stores a word and updates the checksum in one microinstruction.

check.transcript: The disk task stores a word and updates the checksum in one microinstruction.

N14.text: Ethernet sends a bit every two cycles — hence 2.94 megabits — and its random backoff is read off the refresh counter.

N15.text: Switch the screen off, and programs run almost three times faster.

check.transcript: Switch the screen off, and programs run almost three times faster.

N16.text: All four display tasks together? Sixty-three microinstructions. Your program? Task zero. It gets whatever's left.
